Sarah vit au Canada depuis 25 ans. Cette: Sarah has lived in Canada for 25 years. The woman, who is in her forties, grew up near Paris. Her parents, Jews from Algeria, returned to France when Algeria became independent. She is a mother of five.
Hajer, qui habite au Canada depuis quatr: Hajer, who has lived in Canada for four years, was born in Kuwait in 1984. Her Palestinian parents fled the West Bank during the Six-Day War in 1967. They eventually settled in Jordan. She is a mother of three.
La Converse a rencontré ces deux femmes,: La Converse met these two women, a Sephardic Jew and a Palestinian, at various public gatherings related to the Israeli-Palestinian issue. Although they don’t agree on everything, one thing unites them: these mothers realize that people are dying on both sides. Both call for humanity for both peoples.

<strong>Jeudi 12 octobre.</strong> Devan: Thursday, October 12. In front of Scotia Tower, in downtown Montréal, the organization Palestinian and Jewish Unity (PAJU) is holding its weekly vigil. As the rain begins to fall, activists hold up their signs and flags and hand out pamphlets calling for a boycott of Israel and an end to apartheid. Most passersby keep walking, indifferent. Some offer sympathetic smiles, while others call PAJU members “terrorists.” Someone spits on the Palestinian flag.
Sarah* se tient sur le côté de la rue, p: Sarah* stands at the side of the street, perplexed. “Do you agree with all of this?” she asks me. She holds her phone, displaying images of sheets stained with the blood of Israeli victims. “Boycott Israel and end apartheid? I find that rather paradoxical, given PAJU’s claim of unity between Jews and Palestinians. There’s a certain dichotomy here,” she laments.
Une des pancartes du PAJU appelle au boy: One of the PAJU signs calls for a boycott of apartheid in Israel. Photo by Djazia Bousnina.
Depuis l’attaque du Hamas sur le territo: Since the Hamas attack on Israeli territory, Sarah has been deeply shaken. “I have no appetite anymore, I can’t sleep. I’m not Israeli, but I’m Semitic, I’m Jewish. To me, it feels like an offence against my own family,” she confides, her voice sad.
Des larmes perlent de ses yeux lorsqu’el: Tears well up in her eyes as she explains: “I think that as a people, Jews often tend to keep a low profile because of the history of our persecution. We feel like we constantly have to justify ourselves.” Her lower lip trembles, she lowers her eyes to the ground, then continues: “But what’s happening now is undeniably and categorically unacceptable. It’s a violation of every moral limit. When I look at these images – children’s beds covered in blood (...) – it’s beyond comprehension.”
Des membres de l'organisation Palestinie: Members of the organization Palestinian and Jewish Unity (PAJU) in front of Scotia Tower, in the heart of downtown Montréal. They hold a sign showing a Palestinian child killed on a beach in Gaza. Photo: Djazia Bousnina
Son regard s’arrête sur l’affiche du PAJ: Her gaze settles on the PAJU poster showing a lifeless Palestinian child on a beach in Gaza. She shakes her head in disagreement. “I can’t believe they’re talking to me about their dead! We have to defend ourselves. We are not the aggressors. We are not the ones who start the aggression; rather, we are constantly forced to respond to attacks directed against us. As Jews, we are deeply rooted in pacifist values. We don’t want war, we want to restore peace,” says Sarah. She mentions videos from the Palestinian Red Crescent released after the attacks on Gaza. The organization is asking for help to support civilian victims of the bombings. “Hamas should use its money to help its poor people instead of using it to destroy us!” she hammers out, turning her back on us.

<strong>Vendredi 13</strong> <strong>oct: Friday, October 13. I meet Hajer. She stands in the heart of the Montréal tide that has come to show its support for Palestine. A black-and-white keffiyeh draped over her shoulders, she wears a black thobe (dress) adorned with Palestinian embroidery.
Quelques heures avant la manifestation,: A few hours before the demonstration, Hajer went to the library to print posters bearing the slogan “Free Palestine.” “A woman with a child wearing a kippah complained about me and asked the library to refuse to serve me. She thought my posters were antisemitic and glorified terrorism. Fortunately, the library rejected her request,” she says.
« On m’a dit qu’il pouvait être dangereu: “I was told it could be dangerous to come to the demonstration, but for my children and me, it’s the only place where we feel safe. I feel like I’m exactly where I need to be right now, with these thousands of people. It fills me with hope, I’m proud to see this mobilization,” she tells me, sweeping her gaze over the streets overrun by a crowd of demonstrators.
Des policiers sont postés devant le Cons: Police officers are posted in front of the Consulate General of Israel in Montréal to ensure security in case things get out of hand. Photo: Quentin Dufranne
Sur les marches du Consulat général d’Is: On the steps of the Consulate General of Israel, helmeted police officers are on alert, ready to intervene. Seeing them, Hajer says: “I can’t imagine what it must be like in Jerusalem, to pray under the watch of the Israeli army. I feel uneasy even now; I can’t imagine how hard it must be.”
Un sourire se dessine sur ses lèvres. El: A smile forms on her lips. She continues, determined: “My fellow Palestinians have always told me that they find comfort in knowing that we haven’t forgotten them, that we hold our elected officials to account, that we denounce this injustice,” she says of Israel’s bombings of Gaza.
Hajer regrette l’amalgame qui est fait p: Hajer deplores the conflation some politicians make between the demonstrations, Hamas, terrorism and Palestine: “I no longer want to spend my time justifying ourselves. I’m tired of defending the humanity of my people, of my faith. It’s exhausting!”
Elle prend une profonde respiration et c: She takes a deep breath and continues: “They’re trying to make people believe we rejoice in the death of children. That’s false! No one can rejoice in the death of children. At the same time, this situation only gets talked about when the victims are Israeli. Where is the international community when Israeli soldiers <l1>kill children</l1> in the West Bank? At least <l2>34</l2> children were killed <l3>from January to August 2023</l3>. There is no Hamas in the West Bank; no justification can be found for shooting at children.”
Un réfugié de Gaza demande aux manifesta: A refugee from Gaza asks demonstrators to turn on their phones so the sea of people can be seen more clearly. Photo: Quentin Dufranne
La manifestation tire à sa fin. Au mégap: The demonstration is winding down. A Gaza refugee who arrived in Montréal five years ago speaks through a megaphone. He begins by stating that there are Palestinian Jews, Muslims and Christians. Then, to honour the memory of Gazans who are dying without funerals, he recites a prayer – for the dead, but also for the living – so that they may endure the atrocities they are living through. He ends this collective prayer, delivered in front of the Consulate of Israel, by asking forgiveness for his people, for their dead and for all Palestinian and Israeli victims. “اللهم اغفر لموتانا ولجميع الموتى” (O God, have mercy on our dead, and on all the dead), the speaker declares. Hajer’s lips softly form an “amin” (amen).

<strong>Mardi 17</strong> <strong>octobr: Tuesday, October 17. Hajer welcomes me into her home in Côte-Saint-Luc. News has just broken of the bombing of a hospital in Gaza. At the time of writing, no independent official investigation has yet determined who is responsible for this tragedy.
Pour Hajer, cela ne fait aucun doute : l: For Hajer, there is no doubt: the Israeli army is responsible for this strike against civilians. “People in Gaza are reporting hundreds of deaths. It’s not the first time Israel has targeted a hospital. <l1>We haven’t forgotten 2014</l1>,” she recalls, her eyes full of emotion. “I feel guilty being here, safe with my three children, while in Gaza there are hundreds of thousands of people in danger of death,” Hajer confides.
« <em>Gaza ! Gaza ! Don’t you cry, we wi: “Gaza! Gaza! Don’t you cry, we will never let you die,” Hajer sings with her eyes closed. “You simply can’t compare the horrors that Israeli settlers inflict on Palestinians to the October 7 attack. For decades, they’ve been destroying their trees, stealing their land, taking their homes. All of this started well before October 7. They claim they want to establish peace, but what peace are we talking about? For whom? Palestinians haven’t known peace since 1948. And when people say we’re at war… This isn’t a war, it’s a massacre, an ethnic cleansing, a genocide of the Palestinian people! Peace will remain out of reach as long as there is no Palestinian state, as long as Palestinians can’t get their land back and prosper at home… There will be no peace as long as Israel persists,” she adds after a long silence.
Hajer se souvient de ses visites chez sa: Hajer remembers visiting her grandmother in the West Bank: broken windows, bullets lodged in the walls, and her grandmother tending her olive trees. “My maternal grandparents always refused to leave their land. They resisted all their lives, preferring to live in danger rather than in exile. My grandfather was killed by the Israeli army during the First Intifada. My grandmother died 30 years later, at the age of 90. She was older than the State of Israel. She was born free but she died colonized.”
Sa voix tremble, son calme s’évapore : «: Her voice trembles, her calm evaporates: “We are not people inclined to violence. Why did Gaza not stir any interest in <l1>2018-2019</l1>? When the people of Gaza marched peacefully toward the border every Friday, and more than <l2>200</l2> <l3>people</l3>, including <l4>an infant of 8</l4> <l5>months, lost their lives</l5>? We don’t have to look far to identify the victims, to understand who is oppressed and who is the oppressor. All you have to do is look at who controls the water and access to medical care,” she says.
« Tout ce que je désire, c’est revenir d: “All I want is to return to my country in peace, without the constant fear of being exterminated. It’s hard to justify the validity of a murderous state, a state that caused my exile and that of my people. I’m not trying to make the Jews leave, but rather to bring back all Palestinians.”
La porte de la maison s’ouvre, laissant: The front door opens, letting in her son. After a warm salam (an Arabic greeting meaning “Peace be upon you”), the 13-year-old, born in Jordan, looks at his mother with concern and asks: “Did you see what happened at the hospital? Did you see the children? Will there be another demonstration this week? We have to go!”
Hajer l’embrasse sur la joue et reprend: Hajer kisses him on the cheek and continues: “They say the old will die off and the young will forget, but we’re still here. Our very existence is an act of resistance. You know, I’ve never seen my son as passionate as he was at last week’s demonstration.”
L’adolescent enchaîne : « Je me sentais: The teenager picks up: “I felt full of energy, I felt strong. On the Monday after the weekend of October 7, my teacher called Palestinians ‘terrorists.’ This week, she backed down after seeing the reaction from students and parents. Now she says every human being deserves to live.”
« Mon fils n’a jamais mis les pieds en P: “My son has never set foot in Palestine,” says Hajer, “but we intend to go next summer, hoping there will still be a Palestine to go back to.”

<strong>Mercredi 18</strong> <strong>oct: Wednesday, October 18. At the corner of Saint-Laurent Boulevard and Duluth Avenue East, pasted on a pole, a poster shows a young Israeli woman abducted by Hamas on October 7. A few steps away, Sarah waits for me in a café. More than 11 days after the Hamas attacks in Israel and the Netanyahu government’s retaliation against Gaza, Sarah’s tone is more nuanced.
« C’est tout simplement horrible, tout c: “It’s just horrible, everything that’s happening in Gaza.” It is the day after the bombing of Al-Ahli Baptist Hospital in Gaza. Sarah is convinced that it was a Palestinian rocket that fell on the hospital. “Hamas hides in schools, mosques and hospitals. And yesterday, it bombed its own people!” she says.
La paix est-elle encore possible, malgré: Is peace still possible, despite everything? Sarah hesitates.
« Cette guerre sera longue. Aujourd’hui,: “This war will be long. Today, I don’t believe dialogue is possible. But maybe one day, in two or three generations, when tensions have eased, I think we’ll get there. In the immediate term, the loss of human life has to stop,” she says.
Pour elle, les attaques du Hamas ont res: For her, the Hamas attacks have tightened the bonds among Jews and strengthened their loyalty to Israel. “Do you know what it’s like to live constantly among people who barely tolerate you? Six million Jews were exterminated. The world needs Israel. It’s a necessity. If Israel had always existed, there would have been no Holocaust,” she exclaims.
Elle ouvre l’application Instagram sur s: She opens the Instagram app on her phone to share a <l1>video</l1> illustrating solidarity within the Jewish community. It shows an IDF soldier lying on white bags that appear to contain donations, a cigarette in his mouth, one in his nose and two more behind his ears, saying in Hebrew: “Thank you for everything you’re sending, but we don’t need anything else.” She comments with a smile: “Hamas tried to destroy us, but it made us stronger. The Jewish community is incredibly united and resilient.”
Elle repense aux mesures prises par le g: She thinks back to the measures taken by the Israeli government in response to the Hamas attack, which left 1,400 victims. Regarding the water and electricity cuts Israel imposed on the people of Gaza, Sarah wonders: “Why aren’t Palestinians self-sufficient? Why don’t Palestinians have their own water and their own electricity? Why do they depend on Israel? Me, if something like that ever happened to me, forget it! I’d figure it out on my own!”
Nous abordons la question du siège de Ga: We turn to the siege of Gaza, which has already been under blockade since 2007. Her gaze softens, and she admits: “The truth – and I realize it’s not fair – is that I was never really interested in the problems of Palestinians before.”
Au sujet des 34 enfants palestiniens qui: On the 34 Palestinian children killed in the West Bank from January to August 2023, she explains: “I’ve heard about teenagers throwing stones at moving vehicles, smashing windows and causing drivers to lose control and crash. That’s why the Israel Defense Forces have to intervene.”
Elle secoue sa bouteille de jus d’orange: She shakes her bottle of orange juice. A few seconds of silence pass. Then she adds: “Palestinians need to be okay. They need to be able to live in peace. They need to be able to settle, to feel good, so they too can have normal lives.” She brings up France: “It’s the same. I grew up in a neighbourhood in the Paris suburbs. Recently, there were major riots after the killing of <l1>Nahel</l1>, a young Muslim who was killed by police. In response, <l2>young people destroyed public property.</l2> But why did they do all that damage?” she asks rhetorically. “Because they’re not accepted. When you’re not accepted, when there’s no equality, that’s what happens. It’s the same for Palestinians. Every parent wants to be able to raise their family, to give their children opportunities, a future. You want to be able to raise your children, you want them to be able to live well, to have a chance at life; and there, that’s not there.”
Sarah estime aujourd’hui qu’il est fonda: Sarah now believes it is fundamental that Palestinians live in decent conditions for peace to be envisioned in the region. “To have that peace, we Jews also need to be respected and valued in the Middle East,” she adds.
Dans ces moments difficiles, Sarah trouv: In these difficult times, Sarah finds refuge in her faith. I then mention to her the last line of the collective prayer recited during the demonstration in support of Palestine. “O God, have mercy on our dead, and on all the dead.” Moved, Sarah takes out her phone and in turn recites the Torah to me. Psalm 122 of David: “Pray for the peace of Jerusalem! May those who love you live in security! May peace be within your walls and tranquility in your palaces,” she concludes.
Sarah et Hajer ne se prénomment pas réel: Sarah and Hajer aren’t really named that. They wish to remain anonymous for security reasons. I chose to give them these names because both of them spoke to me about their shared religious heritage, of which <l1>Sarah</l1> and <l2>Hajar</l2> are emblematic figures.
